Money is always important, particularly to a have-not province, but whatever payments are made under this bill or any other measure will depend largely upon the spirit and attitudes we develop toward each other as separate parts of a great nation which has been so appropriately designated a dominion. This, in turn, will depend upon our ideas, our concepts and comprehension of what confederation was meant to be and what it actually has become. An act of parliament can join two countries together, but it cannot achieve unity and a nation without unity is like an empty shell without the all important kernel; it looks all right on the outside but the vital seed, life powers so essential to future growth and development, is missing.
The act of union of 1840 is a fine example of this. It joined together Upper and Lower Canada into a union which Sir John A. Macdonald himself referred to in a speech at Halifax as nominal only. When we Canadians discuss national unity we are prone to think mostly in terms of French speaking and English speaking Canadians. This is certainly a very important aspect of the problem as the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet (Mr. Fortin) pointed out in his excellent address at the opening of this session. But equally important, and equally difficult to solve, is the problem of unity between English speaking Canadians in general and between the nine English speaking provinces in particular. It is right and proper that we should work to achieve unity with our French speaking compatriots. But should we overlook the necessity of putting forth any effort to achieve unity amongst ourselves? In the absence of a language barrier, for some unaccountable reason we assume that unity follows automatically. Nothing could be further from the truth.
The whole course of our history since confederation proves the fallacy of that assumption. If we need any further proof we need only go back to the dominion-provincial fiscal conference in 1957. Anyone who analyses the speeches made by the 10 provincial premiers on that occasion could only conclude that far from having a national concept, we think and act as if Canada were merely a group of separate states joined together by the Canadian National Railways and the C.B.C. Perhaps we should not be surprised at this because if we look back through the corridors of our history we find that it was ever thus.

The dominion-provincial conference to which I referred a minute ago only confirmed that we have made very little real progress toward genuine national unity. Such unity as we appear to have is more glitter than gold, more shadow than substance. It may appear genuine on the surface, but if we are honest we must admit it does not run very deep; our divisions are still very real. They arise primarily out of mutual suspicion and mistrust.

There was distrust of the motives of the two Canadas when they approached the maritime provinces and held out to them this vision of a Canadian nation. This distrust, unhappily, has been confirmed over and over again by the actions and attitudes of the central provinces during the past 80 years. Hon. members who have been indoctrinated with the myth that the poor down and out Atlantic provinces sought union with Canada for their own benefit may be surprised to learn that it was Canada, and not the maritimes, who made the first approach. These are historical facts. The reasons are quite clear. The maritimes could get along without Canada, but for central Canada confederation was an absolute necessity.
To refresh our minds let us go back in history to the period in which confederation first took place. At that time the British North American colonies were divided into two isolated groups separated by hundreds of miles of uninhabited wilderness from Upper and Lower Canada in central Canada to the maritime provinces on the eastern seaboard. The British government was very anxious that the North American colonies should take some responsibility for their own defence, and to do this some form of union between them was necessary. It was in this setting that the British North American colonies found themselves in the year 1864, and for the benefit of my hon. friend if he cannot contain his patience, I refer to this because it affords an interesting parallel between the experience of Newfoundland and the experience of the other maritime provinces since confederation.
In 1864 the maritime provinces began taking steps to form a confederation of their own. It was a propitious time. The maritime provinces were enjoying unprecedented prosperity based on their shipbuilding industry, their shipping industry and a lucrative foreign trade.
They had developed sound economies with both Nova Scotia and New Brunswick budgeting for surpluses of nearly half a million dollars. That is not exactly hay even in these days, but in those days it was something relatively huge. With their public debt of about $13 per head, their financial position generally was sound and capital was flowing in to develop their natural resources. Mines were being opened up, manufacturing industries were being established and prosperity was growing. Recognizing the threat to their security and bearing in mind that union had brought prosperity to the colonies in the

Grants to Newfoundland south, in 1864 they took the first steps towards bringing about a maritime confederation.
It was then that Sir John A. Macdonald and Hon. George Etienne Cartier arrived on the scene with their vision of a British North American nation and their proposal that the maritime provinces should unite with them to bring it about. As a further inducement they held out the prospects of the maritime provinces becoming the Massachusetts of British North America. The manufacturing industries of the maritimes would supply the agricultural economy of central Canada. The intercolonial railway which the maritime provinces had planned to build for themselves would be extended to Montreal and Toronto, with central Canada bearing the largest cost. Thus maritime coal would have a market in central Canada and the maritime provinces would provide a market for central Canada beef and farm produce. In addition to this domestic trade, all the foreign trade of the confederated provinces was going to flow through maritime ports; and Halifax and Saint John, New Brunswick were destined to take their place among the great emporiums of the world. These promises were all outlined in speeches by Sir John A. Macdonald and Hon. George Etienne Cartier as they toured the maritime capitals, and they are a matter of record.
This idea of a British North American nation appealed to the patriotic instincts of the maritime people but they were frankly sceptical of the purity of the motives that prompted it. They had heard of the old saying "Beware of the Greeks, especially when they come bringing gifts". They knew that Upper and Lower Canada were enjoying a measure of prosperity but they knew also that it was based largely on trade with the United States which would diminish, if not disappear, when the civil war ended. They knew that the population of Upper Canada, like their own, had been greatly increased by the influx of Loyalists from the United States. They were aware that while the population of the two Canadas was over three times as great as theirs combined, yet the per capita public debt was $65 as compared with theirs of $13.
They were aware that the two Canadas themselves were joined together in a union which was so imcompatible that it could not possibly work and would have to be dissolved. They were conscious of the fact that the St. Lawrence seaway, frozen up five months or six months out of the year, made the two Canadas dependent on the United States for an outlet to the sea. This made them particularly vulnerable to pressure from the United States which could force them into political union simply by denying them access to the

sea. The maritime leaders knew that without access to the sea the economic life of the two Canadas would be severely restricted, if not completely strangled and that unless the maritimes confederated with them the two Canadas could never of themselves become a nation and would eventually be absorbed into the United States economy.
They saw that Upper and Lower Canada had nothing to lose and everything to gain from their proposals while the maritimes had much to lose, including their industries and their prosperity, because they would become a captive market, and whatever benefits they received would depend entirely on the good faith of the people and the government of central Canada. Consequently they had misgivings; and so for them confederation would be an act of faith.
But the maritime provinces, like Newfoundland, had one vulnerable spot. Their Achilles heel was an overwhelming patriotism and loyalty to the British crown and British traditions. For the sake of ensuring that North America would remain within the British commonwealth, in 1867 they finally entered into union. They knew it would involve some sacrifice and they were prepared to make it out of loyalty and patriotism in order to preserve British influence in North America.
But they saw too that the vision of a British nation in North America could become a reality and that their prosperity need not be impaired-and could even be improved- provided that the central provinces were sincere and would live up to their side of the bargain. So they came into confederation fully realizing, that like Newfoundland they were putting themselves completely at the mercy of central Canada whose larger representation would control the federal government and their only protection was sincerity, good will and good faith on the part of those whose proposals they had accepted.
Ninety years have now passed and to what extent has that faith been justified? What is the verdict of history? I am not going to take the time of the house to deal with that matter because we know what has happened. We know what world emporiums are on the Atlantic seaboard. We know what has happened to the shipping industry, the shipbuilding industry and to the prosperity of the maritimes. The answers to all these questions are recorded in history and they prove that the scepticism and fears of the people of the maritimes were well founded when the Upper Canada "Greeks" appeared with their gifts and promises.
Once their dependence on the United States had been removed; once their means of defence had been organized and a line of

defence communications set up to make possible supplies and reinforcements from the mother country; and once the outlets on the Atlantic seaboard had been secured to permit expansion of their trade and commerce, central Canada had little further use for the maritimes, and the great national vision became concentrated within the confines of Upper and Lower Canada.
No blame is to be attached to the ordinary people of those days because they were uninformed. Mass communications were few and far between and were poor in quality. But the federal government of the day certainly knew what was going on and it is on them that the blame must be placed. The big business interests of central Canada had no intention whatever of permitting strong competitive economies to develop on the eastern seabord and they succeeded in bringing to bear on the federal government sufficient pressure to ensure the success of their plans.
It was not long before the maritime provinces-deprived of their trading advantages, forced to buy in a captive market, victims of preferential tariffs designed to protect the industries and economy of central Canada to which their own economies had been made prisoner-began to assume the status of poor relations dependent upon the bounty and generosity of their sister provinces. That is the way that confederation has worked in the past. I ask the Minister of Finance whether that is the way in which he wants it to work in the years to come.
Newfoundland did not have any part in this great North American drama but she was a very interested spectator. She did not send delegates to the Charlottetown conference when the maritime confederation was being discussed, but she did send two delegates- Hon. F. B. T. Carter and Hon. Ambrose Shea- to the Quebec conference where the resolutions embodying the terms of the larger union were drawn up.
These terms were so unacceptable that Newfoundland rejected them outright, as indeed did Prince Edward Island and the other maritime provinces. In New Brunswick the proponents of confederation were so roundly defeated in a provincial election that Dr. Tupper, the Conservative leader, dared not risk an election in Nova Scotia on the same issue and the people of Nova Scotia to this day have never had a chance to vote on that issue.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. R. Granger (Grand Falls-While Bay-Labrador):
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE ADDITIONAL GRANTS TO NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising to oppose this bill, and I am opposing it because it destroys one of the terms of the union of Newfoundland with Canada, and distorts the meaning of this union.
What are the terms of union? The terms of union are a solemn treaty entered into between the high contracting powers. They are a solemn contract and covenant entered into between two sovereign nations. They were signed by our representatives. They were signed by representatives of Canada. They were solemnly ratified by the parliament of Canada. As was then necessary, they were ratified by the United Kingdom parliament, and then they became part of the British North America Act, the fundamental law of Canada, the bulwark of the confederation.
It is in the British North America Act that the rights of the provinces are defined and established and set down for all time. It is to the British North America Act that Prince Edward Island looks to preserve its identity and its autonomy. It is to the British North America Act that the French Canadian looks to safeguard his language, his religion and his culture. The British North America Act is the link that crosses the Rockies and ties in British Columbia with the rest of Canada. This great sprawling nation, with all its differences, geographical, historic, climatic, ethnic, is kept together by the British North America Act and of course by the monarchy. And the terms of union are part of the British North America Act, and term 29 is part of the terms of union.
By term 29 Canada is supposed to enable Newfoundland to continue the public services at the levels and standards reached eight years after confederation without having to resort to unreasonable or unreasonably onerous taxation. As I see it, term 29 is a contract, a contractual obligation to use the Prime Minister's words. Under it there was on the part of Canada an undertaking, a guarantee that come what might, Canada would never allow the public services in Newfoundland to go below the level in 1957. Come what might, Canada would enable Newfoundland to continue our public services at the levels and standards then reached.
Of course, Newfoundland was to impose provincial taxation as heavy as the maritime average to continue the public services at these levels but if she was unable to do so without resorting to taxation more burdensome than the maritime average then Canada would provide the difference. How? By giving the additional assistance required. How


much? As much as required. For how long? For as long as required. Not for five years or for fifty years but as long as required.
The royal commission was appointed and it sat and it made its recommendations. The sum of $8 million a year was recommended. The commission established two extremely important points. In the first place it clearly recognized a contract, a contractual obligation, a financial responsibility to Newfoundland on the part of Canada. Secondly, it put no time limit upon it: "and thereafter $8 million". There was dissatisfaction with the report but no one questioned its legality. What was questioned was its generosity, its lack of imagination. After all, it is quite possible to be legal without being generous.
Take a man's legal obligations to his children embracing food, clothing, shelter, and a minimum of education. A man without a heart or soul could discharge his legal obligations at low financial cost but no one would call such a man a generous man. A man's legal obligation toward his wife or his aged parents can be set at a minimum level in terms of dollars and cents but a man who set himself such standards would not be a very admirable character. There was another cause for dissatisfaction. The commission had set a specific amount with no attempt to make provision for changing events or circumstances in the future. Surely, we said, there should be provision for an escalator clause or a periodic review. That was ten months ago. And then the Prime Minister intervened. Why? Because, he said, of the dissatisfaction in Newfoundland. Many Newfoundlanders were elated. After all, if a man notices dissatisfaction and has the power to allay it, the natural assumption is that he will allay it, unless of course he intended all the time to kick us in the teeth.
That was ten months ago. The delay caused Newfoundland financial embarrassment. Over $13 million which was due the province immediately was withheld. In order to continue public services at standards and levels then obtaining Newfoundland had to borrow the money from the bank at 6 per cent. But after all, many Newfoundlanders said, it was worth it. The government of Canada was now considering the case and all would be well. Here was our chance to see a great human document which would put the final seal on the act of confederation. After all, it is not every day in the week that a new nation is born. Here was a chance for vision and magnanimity. The government of Canada was rich in vision; they had told us so. The Prime Minister had great visions about the undeveloped parts of Canada and was most anxious to see that they should have proper

levels and standards of public services. Here was a chance for generosity and sympathy. The way many thought the government of Canada would allay our dissatisfaction would be to take the bare bones of the contract and breathe the breath of life into it and make it a warm and living thing. What they actually did to allay our dissatisfaction was to take our contract, tear it into pieces and throw it back in our face. It was a gross betrayal.
Legalities have been mentioned but more than legalities are needed. If I understand history correctly nations are not built on technicalities. Nations grow in strength and greatness because of a union of hearts, and because of mutual understanding and aid between the various peoples who make up the whole. The measure of a nation's destiny can be gauged by the greatness of the comprehension of the peoples and their leaders of the mutual interests involved.
In term 29 the nation of Canada and the people of Newfoundland pledged their mutual faith in each other and left it for other people of similar goodwill to complete the union which they had begun. It is a pity that this final part of the creation of a mighty modern nation which should be a bright moment in its history should be tarnished by bad faith. It is degrading to see those who are walking with history attempt to reduce a great moment in a nation's development to the lowest common denominator in dollars and cents.
But the final act is not yet over. The time will come, and come it will, when those of us on this side of the house will be in a position to rectify this wrong being done today and justice will be done to the province of Newfoundland by a Liberal government of the future.

Mr. Speaker, we have before us Bill No. C-72 which in my opinion is a complete and definite denial of the constitutional rights of Newfoundland. I said yesterday and I repeat now that term 29 gave to Newfoundland some special rights under the terms of union. I say that it was a special term because it was an agreement made between two countries. My friend the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) quibbles about whether or not Newfoundland at that time was a sovereign country, but at least Canada and Newfoundland were two separate countries within the British commonwealth and had the right to make an agreement as to union between them. I believe that those terms of union which included term 29 represented a solemn declaration between two separate countries to enter into a union.
Grants to Newfoundland
I believe that term 29 is an agreement altogether different from any entered into between the central government and a province, after Newfoundland became a province. If we examine the tax agreement contained in article 27 of the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada we find there are five subsections. The first begins with these words:
The government of Canada will forthwith after the date of union-
The second begins:
The offer to be made under this term-
The third begins with these words:
The offer of the government of Canada to be made under this term-
The fifth commences:
If the province of Newfoundland enters into a tax agreement-
In every case with one exception we find that the agreement entered into between the central government of Canada and the province of Newfoundland as regards tax agreements refers to that period after Newfoundland had become a province of Canada. Term 29 was a different agreement altogether. I believe it was a solemn undertaking between the two parties and if any change is to be made in term 29 it should be made by agreement between the two parties.
I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) yesterday and today as he talked about the fairness and the fair play which he would like the government to give to Newfoundland. I believe he was sincere. I heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) use the same argument. I think he was sincere but I want to point out that the concept of fair play, surely, is not all on one side. I believe that if the two parties concerned in this agreement were to get together now or in the future it would be found that both parties have a concept of fair play which would result in a proper decision being reached between the two parties; but in the present situation we have a unilateral action taken by the government which destroys, eliminates and extinguishes this special right that was given to Newfoundland in the terms of union.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance in his opening remarks placed on Hansard at page 5901 a table showing all the payments that had been made to Newfoundland from the year 1949 to the estimated payments for 1959-60. To place only this table on Hansard may very well leave the impression in the minds of some people that these were special grants and that no grants under similar headings were made to other provinces. But what I would like to see here, and I would hope that during the committee stage the Minister

Grants to Newfoundland of Finance would be prepared to provide this information, is a similar table for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and maybe one of the western provinces. I would like to see a table showing the amount of money that has been collected in Newfoundland under income tax, corporation tax, succession duties and customs and excise, to show that the amounts of money which are included in this table which the Minister of Finance placed on record are only one side of the coin. There is another side showing the amount of money which has been collected over those years in the province of Newfoundland. I should like to have a further look at these figures.
My hon. friend from St. John's West compared the amount of unconditional grants for the year 1957-58 with the year 1958-59. The total amount of unconditional grants, according to this table, for the year 1957-58 was $19,244,000. For the year 1958-59, according to this table, the total amount of unconditional grants was $40,847,000. The Minister without Portfolio says that here is an increase of over 100 per cent; but let me point out something here.
